title: How to plan 20 delivery stops when no computer can
description:
A van with 20 stops has 20!/2, about 1.2 quintillion, possible round trips: more than the seconds since the Big Bang, and 38 years of work at a billion routes a second. So drivers' software doesn't try them all. Start with the greedy route (always go to the nearest stop left), which is fast but crosses itself; on the 9-stop map in this video it's 24% longer than the best loop. Then find two roads that cross and reverse the stretch between them: by the triangle inequality the uncrossed loop is always shorter. Repeat until no crossing is left (the 2-opt method): here that lands within 3% of the best. UPS's ORION system plans routes of about 100 stops a day per driver and UPS credits it with cutting about 100 million miles a year.

Numbers checked in code: 20!/2, the 38 years, 100,000 random crossings (uncrossing was always shorter), and the demo map solved exactly (Held-Karp). Sources: Wikipedia, Travelling salesman problem; FreightWaves on UPS ORION.

social_caption: 20 delivery stops have more possible routes than seconds since the Big Bang. Here's the trick delivery software uses to find a short one anyway.
facts_checked: Depot + 20 stops: 20!/2 = 1,216,451,004,088,320,000 round trips (1.2 quintillion), 2.8x the 4.35e17 seconds since the Big Bang (13.787 billion years); at a billion a second, 38.5 years (verify.py)
Nearest neighbour heuristic: always go to the nearest unvisited city; on random maps it averages about 25% longer than the best (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travelling_salesman_problem)

2-opt: remove two edges and reconnect the other way; any tour with crossings can be made shorter without them (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travelling_salesman_problem); 100,000 random crossings, uncrossing always shorter (verify.py)
Demo map (depot + 9 stops): nearest neighbour 2,833 vs best 2,283 (Held-Karp) = 24% longer, 2 crossings; two flips: 2,646 then 2,357, no crossings, 3.2% over the best (verify.py)
UPS ORION: a typical driver day is about 100 stops; the software cuts about 100 million miles a year (https://www.freightwaves.com/?p=83401, quoting UPS)
CTA: 5 stops in a loop: 4!/2 = 12 (verify.py, brute force)

beats.say: No computer tries them all. At a billion a second, that's 38 years.
You drive the van. Today, 9 stops. You want the shortest loop back home.
Step 1: always drive to the nearest stop you haven't done yet.
It's fast. But look, the route crosses itself. It's 24% longer than the best one.
And that X is the clue. A shortest loop never crosses itself.
Step 2: find two roads that cross, and flip the stretch between them. The loop always gets shorter.
Step 3: repeat until there's no X left. Now you're within 3% of the best.
UPS does this for 100 stops a day, and says it cuts 100 million miles a year.
So, 5 stops. How many different loops can you drive?
